imp.generic: Black Americans have long been denied the rights that were promised to them by the founding documents of the United States.
imp.author: This country made a promise, wrote it down in the most solemn language men could find, and then, before the ink was dry, began the long, elaborate, exhausting project of explaining why the promise did not mean what it said, had never meant what it said, and could not possibly apply to the people who needed it most.

imp.generic: He felt a deep and complicated grief when his father died.
imp.author: When my father died I discovered that grief is not a single country but a continent, and that somewhere in its interior, past the weeping and the eulogies and the decent casseroles left at the door, there lives a rage so old and so particular that you cannot name it without also naming everything the man endured, everything that was taken from him before you ever arrived to take anything yourself.

imp.generic: It was a difficult time to be alive in America.
imp.author: I want to begin by telling you what the air felt like, because the air is where you feel a country first, before the laws reach you, before the words do, and the air in those years had the quality of a held breath, a nation standing at the edge of something it had caused and could not quite bring itself to name.

imp.generic: Love requires honesty, even when honesty is painful.
imp.author: You cannot love a person and lie to them; you can only love the version of them you have constructed to spare yourself the difficulty of the real one, and that is not love, that is decoration, that is what people do with furniture when they cannot bear to live in the actual room.

imp.generic: With that understanding in mind, we can now turn to the question of what must change.
imp.author: And so we arrive, as we always arrive, at the question the country has been postponing since before any of us were born, the question it dresses in the language of complexity and timing and the long arc of history, as though the arc were bending on its own, as though no one's back were breaking against it.

imp.generic: Growing up poor taught him that the world was indifferent to his suffering.
imp.author: What the poverty taught me, what it drove into me the way weather drives into old wood, was not that the world was cruel, exactly, but that the world had made its arrangements without consulting me and saw no particular reason to revise them on my account, and that this indifference was not an accident but a decision, renewed every morning by people who would have been offended to hear it called that.

imp.generic: Silence in the face of injustice makes a person complicit in that injustice.
imp.author: I have heard the silence of good people, and I want you to understand that it is not an empty sound; it is full, it is crowded with everything the good person knows and will not say, and the injustice feeds on it the way a fire feeds on the oxygen in a room, gratefully, without malice, simply because it is there and because silence, whatever its intentions, burns.

imp.generic: He stood at the window and looked out at the city, wondering what his life had amounted to.
imp.author: He stood at the window the way a man stands when he has run out of motion, looking down at the street that had held his whole life like a fist, and he thought, not for the first time, that a city will watch you be born and watch you die and never once change its expression, and that this is either the cruelest thing in the world or the most honest, and he had never, in all his years, been able to decide which.

imp.generic: In the end, what matters most is whether we were willing to tell the truth.
imp.author: What will matter, when the accounting comes, is not whether we were comfortable, not whether we were liked, not whether we managed to get through our lives without disturbing anyone's dinner, but whether, in the moment when the truth required a human voice, we were willing to be that human, willing to stand in the room and say the thing, however it shook us, however it cost us, however completely it burned down the version of ourselves we had been so carefully constructing all those careful years.

imp.generic: America has never fully reckoned with the violence at the heart of its history.
imp.author: The history is not past; that is the first thing, the hardest thing, the thing this country has spent the better part of three centuries refusing to understand, that you cannot bury an atrocity and call the burial a conclusion, that the dead have a terrible patience, that everything the nation has built on the fact of what was done sits on that fact still, and the foundation does not care how many flags you fly above it or how sincerely you have come to believe in your own innocence.
